newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Market boom aids Vereinsbank profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Market boom aids Vereinsbank profits.

text.p: Bayerische Vereinsbank AG on Tuesday said it had set ambitious profit goals for 1997 after buoyant market conditions helped it post an 18 percent rise in 1996 operating earnings.

Chief executive Albrecht Schmidt told a news conference the bank was confident of "building on last year's improved profitability" and said business at the start of 1997 had already surpassed expectations.

The Bavarian mortgage specialist reported operating profits of around 1.6 billion marks ($940 million) for last year -- at the upper end of forecasts -- amid strong advances in interest and commission earnings in what proved a boom year for financial markets.

While Vereinsbank did not release a precise net profit figure for the year, Schmidt said net earnings rose some 30 percent from the previous year's 657 million marks and the bank is to raise its dividend to 1.60 marks per share from 1.50.

Schmidt took the opportunity to repeat that his group, one of the smaller of Germany's Top Five banks, aimed to remain independent. This has become a hot issue since Deutsche Bank last year revealed a 5.2 percent stake in the bank, starting a wave of takeover rumours.
The news gave Vereinsbank's shares an early boost, sending them up to a high of 64.91 marks in early screen trade, but they later slipped back to end bourse trade unchanged at 63.90.
Analysts said the results matched most expectations, although risk provisions -- at 700 million marks little changed from 1995 -- were somewhat lower than expected.
Trinkaus & Burkhardt analyst Markus Strigl said he was keeping a "hold" recommendation on Vereinsbank, whose shares have risen more than a third since mid-1996 on merger talk.
"The shares are too expensive from a fundamental point of view," Strigl commented.
Vereinsbank's growth came on the back of a seven percent rise in net interest income to 4.8 billion marks and a 14 percent increase to 1.2 billion marks in net commission income.
That was supported by low interest rates and modest prices which boosted interest in mortgages, the bank said.
The rise was also accompanied by stagnation on risk provisions and own-account trading income, while administrative expenses rose six percent to 3.9 billion marks.
Strong interest income and commission income were a general feature for all the German banks in 1996, BHF Bank analyst Dieter Hein commented.
"At the same time spending is also generally low, apart from banks like Deutsche and Dresdner, which had to invest in their UK investment banking," Hein said.

Market leader Deutsche also reported a 38 percent rise in operating profit to an unexpectedly high 5.8 billion marks but its net earnings, probably hurt by the costs from a funds scandal at Morgan Grenfell, were stable at 2.2 billion.
Commerzbank AG has already announced a 22 percent rise in net income for the year.
Germany's last two top banks, Dresdner Bank and Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel-Bank AG, will release their data later this week.

Vereinsbank also announced it was setting up for the first time a fund for general banking risks to strengthen its capital base -- a prelude to reporting under International Accounting Standards (IAS) as Deutsche already does.
Vereinsbank said a total of 595 million marks had been allocated to the fund, mostly by unlocking hidden reserves -- a feature of traditional German accounting.
The balance sheet total rose 13 percent to 404 billion marks in 1996 and group lending volume increased 11 percent to around 312 billion. ($ = 1.703 German Marks)
